screens.title: Abstract Classes and Interfaces
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we focus on two core Java tools for abstraction: abstract classes and interfaces. You'll learn what each construct is, why designers choose one over the other, and how Java's rules shape object hierarchies and capabilities. We'll practice refactoring a Shape hierarchy into an abstract base class and add a small Resizable interface to show how behavior can be mixed in. Understanding abstraction reduces duplicated code and clarifies intent: abstract classes express a shared identity with common state or behavior, while interfaces define contracts and allow multiple independent capabilities. I will point out common mistakes, like attempting to instantiate an abstract class or forgetting to implement an inherited abstract method, and show concrete, runnable examples that highlight those compile-time errors so you can recognize them quickly. By the end of this chapter, you will know when to prefer a stable base class and when to define a capability as an interface, and you will be able to apply default and static interface methods introduced in modern Java to support backward-compatible evolution. Consider how this decision affects testability, coupling, and future extensibility as we proceed.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Abstract Classes & Interfaces
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Abstract Classes and Interfaces

Learn how to express shared identity with abstract classes and define reusable capabilities with interfaces. We emphasize practical design choices, compile-time rules, and modern Java features that keep APIs stable.

In this lesson
Abstract classes, interfaces, and when to use each.

Live code examples, refactor exercise, and common compilation errors.

Coming up
Default and static methods in interfaces.

How default methods ease evolution of interfaces.

Practice
Refactor Shape to be abstract and add Resizable.

Hands-on steps and a small main tester are provided.

Concept Map
Abstract Class: share code + state
Interface: define contracts, multiple inheritance of type
Default / static: evolving interfaces safely
A quick visual to anchor the differences before we code.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to state the formal definitions of abstract classes and interfaces, explain their Java-specific rules, and pick the right construct for a design problem. You will identify when a class should be made abstract because it models a general concept that should not be instantiated, and you will also describe how interfaces capture capabilities that many unrelated classes can share. Practically, you will write an abstract base with at least one abstract method, subclass it and implement required behavior, and create an interface with a concrete default method. Finally, you will refactor a Shape example so that Circle and Rectangle inherit shared behavior from an abstract Shape while Circle also implements a Resizable interface. These skills matter because they reduce duplicate code, improve A P I clarity, and prevent brittle designs. As you practice, watch for common pitfalls like forgetting to implement an abstract method or misusing instance fields in an interface. This chapter prepares you to design flexible, maintainable object hierarchies and to use Java 8 features responsibly for interface evolution.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Learning Objectives — Skills Map
Skill progression
  1. Declare abstract classes and methods — create a base that cannot be instantiated and forces subclasses to implement behavior.
  2. Use constructors and shared fields — call super() from subclasses to initialize shared state.
  3. Design interfaces with default/static methods — provide capability contracts and optional shared implementations.
  4. Refactor and test — run a main method to confirm compile-time rules and runtime behavior.
Common pitfalls
  • Trying to instantiate an abstract class causes a compile error.
  • Forgetting to implement every abstract method in a concrete subclass causes a compile error.
  • Expecting interfaces to hold instance state — interface fields are constants only.

screens.title: What is an abstract class?
screens.narratorSegment: An abstract class is a class that you declare with the abstract keyword and that cannot be instantiated directly. Its primary role is to provide a common base for related concrete subclasses, often sharing fields, constructors, and some implemented methods while leaving other behaviors unspecified. Concretely, if you model a generic Shape where the formula for area depends on the specific kind of shape, Shape should be abstract. Abstract methods are declared without a body and force concrete subclasses to implement the required behavior; if a subclass does not provide implementations for all abstract methods, it must itself be declared abstract. Abstract classes may include constructors, which are invoked by subclasses via super(), and they may include instance variables and static members. A common misconception is that abstract implies lacking any implementation; in fact, abstract classes frequently contain useful concrete methods to avoid duplication. For example, a displayColor method can be implemented once in the abstract base while calculateArea remains abstract. When designing, choose an abstract class when you need shared state or behavior among closely related types and when a single inheritance chain is appropriate. To check understanding: can you name a situation where state should be shared by all subclasses? That situation often points to an abstract class.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › What is an abstract class?
Core Concept

Abstract class essentials

An abstract class can contain concrete and abstract methods, constructors, and fields. It sets a shared structure while preventing direct instantiation.

Has constructors — called by subclasses via super()
May contain state (instance variables)
Contains abstract methods that subclasses must implement
Key Takeaway

Abstract classes are for related types that share state or behavior but need some methods implemented by each concrete subclass.

Example
public abstract class Shape {
  String color;

  public Shape(String color) {
    this.color = color;
  }

  public void displayColor() {
    System.out.println("Shape color: " + color);
  }

  public abstract double calculateArea();
}
Common mistake: trying to create new Shape("Red") will produce a compile-time error.
Pro tip: put shared logic in concrete methods to reduce duplication in subclasses.

screens.title: What is an interface?
screens.narratorSegment: An interface defines a contract — a set of methods that a class must implement when it declares implements. Interfaces represent capabilities, like Drivable or Resizable, which many unrelated classes might share. Before Java 8, interface methods were implicitly public and abstract and interfaces could only hold constants. Since Java 8, interfaces may declare default methods with an implementation and static methods tied to the interface itself. Default methods let you add behavior to an interface without forcing every implementing class to change; static methods serve as utilities related to the interface. Interfaces cannot have constructors and cannot maintain instance state; fields are implicitly public static final. Importantly, a class may implement multiple interfaces, giving multiple inheritance of type. That makes interfaces the right choice when you want loose coupling and plug-and-play capabilities. A common misconception is expecting interfaces to carry mutable fields — they cannot. Think of an interface as “can-do” behavior. For example, Drivable declares startEngine, stopEngine and accelerate; a Car implements those methods and may optionally override a default honk method for a vehicle-specific sound. What is an interface? means interfaces define capabilities and allow classes to adopt multiple types while keeping implementation flexible and loosely coupled.. In practical terms, a contract of behavior and a mechanism for multiple inheritance of type. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › What is an interface?
Core Concept

Interface essentials

Interfaces declare a contract of method signatures. Java 8+ adds default and static methods to help evolve interfaces without breaking implementations.

No constructors, cannot be instantiated
Fields are constants: public static final
Supports multiple inheritance of type through implements
Key Takeaway

Use interfaces for capabilities that many different classes may provide, keeping coupling low.

Example
public interface Drivable {
  void startEngine();
  void stopEngine();
  void accelerate(int speed);

  default void honk() {
    System.out.println("Default honk sound!");
  }

  static String getVehicleType() {
    return "Generic Drivable Vehicle";
  }
}
Pro tip: Use default methods sparingly — they are for backward compatibility, not to store state.
Misconception: interface fields are not instance variables; they are constants only.

screens.title: Abstract Class vs Interface
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the contrast between abstract classes and interfaces helps you make practical design choices. Abstract classes are for closely related types where you want to share implementation, state, and constructors. Interfaces express capabilities that many, possibly unrelated, classes can adopt, and they allow multiple inheritance of type. Consider fields: abstract classes can have instance variables and mutable state; interfaces only have constants. For method types, abstract classes can contain fully implemented methods and abstract methods; pre-Java 8 interfaces only declared abstract methods, while Java 8+ interfaces can include default and static methods to ease evolution. Another difference is inheritance: a class can extend only one abstract class but can implement multiple interfaces. Choose an abstract class when the “is-a” relationship is strong and shared state or behavior is needed. Choose an interface when you need loose coupling and the ability to mix capabilities into classes with different inheritance trees. A frequent design error is adding many unrelated behaviors to an abstract class; if behaviors are orthogonal, prefer interfaces. As a quick test, ask whether the concept needs shared state or just a contract — that question typically resolves the choice.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Abstract Class vs Interface
Side-by-side
Abstract Class
  • Can have constructors
  • Can hold instance fields
  • Can include concrete and abstract methods
  • Single inheritance only
Interface (Java 8+)
  • No constructors; no instance state
  • Methods can be abstract, default, or static
  • Multiple inheritance of type via implements
  • Fields are public static final constants
Decision heuristic: if you need shared state or constructors, lean to an abstract class; if you need multiple independent capabilities, choose interfaces.
Design example
Suppose you need Employees with a calculatePay implementation varying by type, but you also want capabilities like Trainable and Managable that some employees may have. Use an abstract Employee base to share common fields and calculatePay as abstract, and define Trainable and Managable as interfaces to mix into any employee type.
Misconception check: using an interface to hold mutable configuration is wrong; interfaces cannot carry mutable instance fields.
Pro tip: prefer many small interfaces that capture focused capabilities rather than monolithic capability interfaces.

screens.title: Refactor: Shape into AbstractShape
screens.narratorSegment: Now we perform the live refactor. Start by marking Shape as abstract and changing calculateArea into an abstract method. This prevents direct instantiation and makes the A P I explicit about what subclasses must implement. The constructor and displayColor method remain implemented so subclasses can reuse initialization and common behavior. For this walkthrough, we examine a modified AbstractShape, then a Circle subclass that extends it and provides calculateArea. Notice how Circle calls super in its constructor to initialize the shared color field. A frequent error during such refactors is leaving the abstract method with a body or forgetting to add the abstract keyword to the class when removing method bodies; Java will complain if a class has an abstract method but is not declared abstract. Another common mistake is attempting to instantiate an abstract class in tests. As you refactor in your codebase, run the compiler early: compile-time errors are helpful guides. Try to run the provided main tester after the refactor to confirm behavior: constructing a Circle, calling calculateArea, then resizing if applicable. This practice reinforces the design and shows the compile-time contracts working as intended.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Refactor: Shape into AbstractShape
Abstract Base
public abstract class AbstractShape {
  String color;

  public AbstractShape(String color) {
    this.color = color;
  }

  public void displayColor() {
    System.out.println("Shape color: " + color);
  }

  public abstract double calculateArea();
}
Concrete Subclass
public class Circle extends AbstractShape {
  double radius;

  public Circle(String color, double radius) {
    super(color);
    this.radius = radius;
  }

  @Override
  public double calculateArea() {
    return Math.PI * radius * radius;
  }
}
Check: compiling after making calculateArea abstract will fail if any concrete subclass does not implement it. Use the compiler message to find unimplemented subclasses quickly.

screens.title: Introduce a Resizable interface
screens.narratorSegment: Next we introduce an interface to represent an orthogonal capability: Resizable. The interface declares void resize(double factor) and optionally includes a default helper method to print a message when resizing. Because interfaces represent 'can-do' behavior, many classes could implement Resizable, whether or not they share a common superclass. We implement Resizable in Circle to change radius by the factor, call the default print method, and then allow the Circle instance to compute a new area. This demonstrates how interfaces allow multiple inheritance of type: Circle already extends AbstractShape and can also implement Resizable without conflict. A common error students make is adding mutable instance fields to an interface; instead, keep any necessary state in the implementing class. Another error is forgetting to mark the class with implements Resizable; without that the compiler won't treat resize as part of the type. After implementing, the main tester can call resize and then calculateArea to see the changed result. This pattern shows how to separate identity and capability cleanly, increasing reuse and reducing coupling between unrelated classes. Introduce a Resizable interface means interfaces capture independent abilities a class can adopt; implement them on classes that already extend a common base when needed.. In practical terms, add a capability and implement it in circle. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Introduce Resizable interface
Steps
  1. Declare public interface Resizable with void resize(double factor).
  2. Optionally add default helper method to announce resizing.
  3. Have Circle implement Resizable and update radius inside resize.
  4. Test by calling resize and calculateArea from main.
Interface + Implementation
public interface Resizable {
  void resize(double factor);

  default void printResizeMessage(double factor) {
    System.out.println("Resizing by factor: " + factor);
  }
}

public class Circle extends AbstractShape implements Resizable {
  double radius;

  public Circle(String color, double radius) {
    super(color);
    this.radius = radius;
  }

  @Override
  public double calculateArea() {
    return Math.PI * radius * radius;
  }

  @Override
  public void resize(double factor) {
    printResizeMessage(factor);
    this.radius *= factor;
  }
}
Note: Circle can extend its abstract base and also implement Resizable because Java allows multiple interfaces. Keep state in the class, not the interface.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Main tester and expected behavior
Main.java (tester)
public class AbstractionDemo {
  public static void main(String[] args) {
    // AbstractShape s = new AbstractShape("Blue"); // Compile error

    Circle myCircle = new Circle("Red", 5.0);
    System.out.println("Initial Circle Area: " + myCircle.calculateArea());
    myCircle.resize(1.5);
    System.out.println("Resized Circle Area: " + myCircle.calculateArea());
    System.out.println("---");

    Rectangle myRectangle = new Rectangle("Green", 10.0, 4.0);
    System.out.println("Rectangle Area: " + myRectangle.calculateArea());
  }
}
Expected output and checks
1. Attempting to instantiate AbstractShape causes a compile-time error. This enforces the abstraction.
2. Circle.calculateArea returns Math.PI * radius * radius. After resize the area increases consistent with radius change.
3. Rectangle does not implement Resizable and therefore cannot be resized by that interface method unless modified.
Tip: Run each change incrementally to isolate compile errors and confirm the contract behavior before adding more features.

screens.title: Design rules and best practices
screens.narratorSegment: Design decisions about using abstract classes or interfaces depend on intent and future evolution. Prefer an abstract class when types are closely related, share a lot of implementation and state, and you want to avoid repeating constructors or fields. Use an interface when you need to express a capability that many different unrelated classes might offer, especially if you want multiple inheritance of type. Keep interfaces small and focused — many small interfaces are easier to compose than one large interface. Use default methods to add non-breaking helper behavior, but avoid placing mutable state in interfaces; put such state in concrete classes. Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Design rules and best practices
Best practices
  • Keep interfaces focused: one capability per interface when possible.
  • Use abstract classes for shared state: constructors and common fields belong to a base class.
  • Use default methods cautiously: they are for backward compatibility, not to store logic that should live in classes.
  • Prefer composition over inheritance: if you can compose capabilities, prefer interfaces and delegation.
Practical checks
Do I need a constructor or shared fields?
Is this just a capability usable by many unrelated types?
Will I need multiple inheritance of type?
Will adding a default method help evolve the API safely?
A good rule: start with interfaces for capabilities. If you find repeated concrete code across classes, extract an abstract base to avoid duplication while keeping interfaces for orthogonal behavior.

screens.title: Compile-time errors and fixes
screens.narratorSegment: Working through common compilation errors helps you internalize Java's rules. One typical error is attempting to instantiate an abstract class; the compiler will state that the class is abstract and cannot be instantiated. The fix is either to instantiate a concrete subclass or to remove the new call. Another frequent issue is creating a subclass that does not implement all inherited abstract methods; the compiler will force you to implement the missing methods or declare the subclass abstract. If you expect an interface to hold mutable fields, you'll find only constants available; remove attempts to mutate such fields and move state into implementing classes. When using default methods, be aware of method conflicts: if two interfaces provide default methods with the same signature, the implementing class must override and resolve the conflict explicitly. Finally, if you forget to add implements Resizable to a class but call resize on a variable typed to Resizable, the compiler will say the method is undefined — ensure types and declarations align. Compile errors are precise; treat them as a design checklist: they reveal missing implementations, wrong modifiers, or mismatched types. Use them to iteratively refine your design.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Compile-time errors and fixes
Common compiler messages
  • Cannot instantiate the type AbstractShape — fix: instantiate a concrete subclass instead.
  • Class must be declared abstract or implement abstract method — fix: implement the missing method or mark class abstract.
  • Cannot assign a value to final variable — fix: do not attempt to mutate interface constants; move state to class fields.
  • Reference to resize is undefined — fix: add implements Resizable or cast to the correct type.
Quick fixes
  1. Read the compiler error; it points to the problematic class and line.
  2. Implement or declare abstract methods appropriately.
  3. Move mutable data out of interfaces into implementing classes.
  4. Override conflicting default methods explicitly if two interfaces clash.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Here are the central ideas to keep in mind. First, an abstract class is used when several related classes share state or implementation but one or more methods must be implemented by each concrete subclass. Second, an interface defines a capability contract that unrelated classes can adopt; Java 8+ adds default and static methods to help evolve interfaces without breaking implementations. Third, a class can extend only one abstract class but can implement multiple interfaces, which supports multiple inheritance of type. These distinctions affect coupling, testability, and A P I evolution. Remember the practical rule: if you need constructors or shared mutable state, prefer an abstract class; if you need loose contractual behavior that many types may provide, prefer an interface. Keep interfaces focused and use default methods only when they simplify backward compatibility. Finally, treat compiler errors as guidance during refactor: the compiler enforces contracts and will direct you to missing implementations or incorrect declarations. Ask yourself after each design: does this concept require shared state, or is it purely a capability? That single question often resolves the choice.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we focus on two core Java tools for abstraction: abstract classes and interfaces. You'll learn what each construct is, why designers choose one over the other, and how Java's rules shape object hierarchies and capabilities. We'll practice refactoring a Shape hierarchy into an abstract base class and add a small Resizable interface to show how behavior can be mixed in. Understanding abstraction reduces duplicated code and clarifies intent: abstract classes express a shared identity with common state or behavior, while interfaces define contracts and allow multiple independent capabilities. I will point out common mistakes, like attempting to instantiate an abstract class or forgetting to implement an inherited abstract method, and show concrete, runnable examples that highlight those compile-time errors so you can recognize them quickly. By the end of this chapter, you will know when to prefer a stable base class and when to define a capability as an interface, and you will be able to apply default and static interface methods introduced in modern Java to support backward-compatible evolution. Consider how this decision affects testability, coupling, and future extensibility as we proceed.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to state the formal definitions of abstract classes and interfaces, explain their Java-specific rules, and pick the right construct for a design problem. You will identify when a class should be made abstract because it models a general concept that should not be instantiated, and you will also describe how interfaces capture capabilities that many unrelated classes can share. Practically, you will write an abstract base with at least one abstract method, subclass it and implement required behavior, and create an interface with a concrete default method. Finally, you will refactor a Shape example so that Circle and Rectangle inherit shared behavior from an abstract Shape while Circle also implements a Resizable interface. These skills matter because they reduce duplicate code, improve A P I clarity, and prevent brittle designs. As you practice, watch for common pitfalls like forgetting to implement an abstract method or misusing instance fields in an interface. This chapter prepares you to design flexible, maintainable object hierarchies and to use Java 8 features responsibly for interface evolution.

This objectives page maps the practical steps you will follow: declare an abstract class with constructors and fields, write an abstract method, and make concrete subclasses implement that method. You will also declare an interface with at least one method and experiment with default and static methods introduced in Java 8. Each objective includes a micro-task you can complete in the provided starter code: change a Shape class to be abstract, implement calculateArea in Circle and Rectangle, add a Resizable interface to Circle, and use the interface's default helper method for a short log. These tasks reinforce the conceptual distinctions: abstract classes allow shared state and constructors; interfaces express capabilities and support multiple inheritance of type. The mini-milestones are intentionally small so you can iterate quickly, catch compile errors, and learn the specific rules Java enforces. Watch for the common misconception that interfaces can hold instance fields — they cannot unless those fields are constants. We'll point that out as you test the code.

An abstract class is a class that you declare with the abstract keyword and that cannot be instantiated directly. Its primary role is to provide a common base for related concrete subclasses, often sharing fields, constructors, and some implemented methods while leaving other behaviors unspecified. Concretely, if you model a generic Shape where the formula for area depends on the specific kind of shape, Shape should be abstract. Abstract methods are declared without a body and force concrete subclasses to implement the required behavior; if a subclass does not provide implementations for all abstract methods, it must itself be declared abstract. Abstract classes may include constructors, which are invoked by subclasses via super(), and they may include instance variables and static members. A common misconception is that abstract implies lacking any implementation; in fact, abstract classes frequently contain useful concrete methods to avoid duplication. For example, a displayColor method can be implemented once in the abstract base while calculateArea remains abstract. When designing, choose an abstract class when you need shared state or behavior among closely related types and when a single inheritance chain is appropriate. To check understanding: can you name a situation where state should be shared by all subclasses? That situation often points to an abstract class.

An interface defines a contract — a set of methods that a class must implement when it declares implements. Interfaces represent capabilities, like Drivable or Resizable, which many unrelated classes might share. Before Java 8, interface methods were implicitly public and abstract and interfaces could only hold constants. Since Java 8, interfaces may declare default methods with an implementation and static methods tied to the interface itself. Default methods let you add behavior to an interface without forcing every implementing class to change; static methods serve as utilities related to the interface. Interfaces cannot have constructors and cannot maintain instance state; fields are implicitly public static final. Importantly, a class may implement multiple interfaces, giving multiple inheritance of type. That makes interfaces the right choice when you want loose coupling and plug-and-play capabilities. A common misconception is expecting interfaces to carry mutable fields — they cannot. Think of an interface as “can-do” behavior. For example, Drivable declares startEngine, stopEngine and accelerate; a Car implements those methods and may optionally override a default honk method for a vehicle-specific sound. What is an interface? means interfaces define capabilities and allow classes to adopt multiple types while keeping implementation flexible and loosely coupled.. In practical terms, a contract of behavior and a mechanism for multiple inheritance of type. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Understanding the contrast between abstract classes and interfaces helps you make practical design choices. Abstract classes are for closely related types where you want to share implementation, state, and constructors. Interfaces express capabilities that many, possibly unrelated, classes can adopt, and they allow multiple inheritance of type. Consider fields: abstract classes can have instance variables and mutable state; interfaces only have constants. For method types, abstract classes can contain fully implemented methods and abstract methods; pre-Java 8 interfaces only declared abstract methods, while Java 8+ interfaces can include default and static methods to ease evolution. Another difference is inheritance: a class can extend only one abstract class but can implement multiple interfaces. Choose an abstract class when the “is-a” relationship is strong and shared state or behavior is needed. Choose an interface when you need loose coupling and the ability to mix capabilities into classes with different inheritance trees. A frequent design error is adding many unrelated behaviors to an abstract class; if behaviors are orthogonal, prefer interfaces. As a quick test, ask whether the concept needs shared state or just a contract — that question typically resolves the choice.

This prevents direct instantiation and makes the A P I explicit about what subclasses must implement. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.
